lines.say: Here is a puzzle. Two different qubits look alike when we measure them the usual way.
Both read zero half the time and one half the time. How can we tell them apart?
Think of polarized sunglasses. They let through light that wiggles their way.
Send in light wiggling on a slant, and upright glasses pass only half.
Tilt the glasses to that slant, and all of it passes.
The light never changed. Only the question the glasses were asking did.
A qubit works the same way. Picture it as an arrow inside a ball.
Measuring asks about one line through the ball, called an axis, usually zero at the top and one at the bottom.
The nearer the arrow is to an end, the more likely that answer.
Our two qubits lie sideways: plus points front, minus points back.
Both sit halfway between top and bottom, so up or down gives fifty fifty.
Ask along the front to back axis instead, and plus always answers front, minus always back.
But real hardware only asks up or down.
So first, a turn called the H gate swaps front and back with up and down.
Now plus reads zero and minus reads one, every time.
Here the picture breaks. A beam can partly pass, but one particle of light passes or it doesn't.
Fifty fifty doesn't mean the qubit is random. Plus is perfectly definite, just not lined up with the question.
A measurement asks about one axis. To ask about another, turn that axis onto up and down first.
